questions.subtopic: 3A1 Risk response options. Insurance and the risk
questions.question: A retailer's risk owner buys a cyber insurance policy that covers breach response costs for its online store. Which statement BEST describes how this changes the breach risk?

options.A: Part of the financial loss shifts, but likelihood and harm remain
options.B: The breach risk leaves the register while the policy is in force
options.C: The policy itself lowers the likelihood of a breach
options.D: Covered costs move to the insurer, and so does accountability for harm

questions.key_concept: Risk transfer, such as insurance, shifts part of the financial impact; it does not reduce likelihood, harm or accountability.
questions.pre_read: Picture a breach happening after the policy is bought, then check each option against what would actually differ.
questions.correct_explanation: Insurance is a transfer response: it shifts part of the financial consequence to the insurer. It reduces neither the likelihood of a breach nor the harm to customers and operations, and the retailer still answers to customers and regulators. That is why the accountability option loses: accountability for the harm cannot be bought. The breach risk stays in the register with its residual rating, and the risk owner keeps monitoring it.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the risk now feels covered. A transferred risk stays in the register with its residual rating, because the breach can still happen and harm customers.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because insurers can require controls as a condition of cover. The policy itself does nothing to make a breach less likely; only controls the retailer runs can do that.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the insurer does pay covered costs. Customers and regulators still hold the retailer accountable for protecting their data, whoever pays.

tips: Eliminate: B and C credit insurance with removing the risk or lowering its likelihood; transfer shifts money only, so the risk stays recorded and just as likely.
Final two: A beats D because transfer moves part of the financial loss, while accountability for the harm stays with the retailer, covered event or not.
Exam cue: when an option says transfer removes the risk or the accountability, treat it as a trap; transfer shifts money, not ownership.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-39 Section 3.3 (Responding to Risk: accept, avoid, mitigate, share or transfer); ISACA Glossary (risk transfer)

questions.subtopic: 3A1 Risk response options. Risk within appetite
questions.question: A logistics firm's shipment-tracking risk, owned by the operations director, is now within appetite, but the IT manager wants an extra monitoring tool for reassurance. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Have the IT manager buy the proposed monitoring tool
options.B: Ask the IT manager to accept the residual risk formally
options.C: Run a cost-benefit analysis of the proposed monitoring tool
options.D: Have the director accept the residual risk on record

questions.key_concept: A risk already within appetite is accepted by its owner and monitored; it does not need further treatment.
questions.pre_read: Find where the risk sits against appetite, and who owns it, before judging the new tool.
questions.correct_explanation: A risk already within appetite needs acceptance and monitoring, not more treatment. The operations director owns the risk, so they accept the residual risk on record, and the analyst then keeps it under watch. The tool is wanted for reassurance, not to close a gap; a cost-benefit study comes in only if the owner chooses further treatment, so analyzing the tool now answers a question the appetite has already settled.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because more monitoring feels safer. Buying a tool for a risk already within appetite takes budget from risks that are still above it.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the IT manager proposed the tool. The operations director owns this business risk, so acceptance is theirs, not IT's.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because cost-benefit is sound practice. It weighs treatments the owner has chosen to consider; a risk already within appetite needs acceptance and monitoring, not new options.

tips: Eliminate: A adds control to a risk already within appetite, and B gives acceptance to IT instead of the director who owns the risk.
Final two: D beats C because, once risk is within appetite, the owner accepts it and it stays under monitoring; a cost-benefit study comes in only if the owner chooses further treatment.
Exam cue: within appetite means accept and monitor; above appetite means treat. Check where the risk sits before weighing any new control.
questions.framework_ref: NIST IR 8286B-upd1 Section 2.3.1 (Risk Acceptance: exposure within risk tolerance is still reported, monitored and managed); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 RA-7 (Risk Response)

questions.subtopic: 3A1 Risk response options. Privacy risk above appetite
questions.question: A hospital's compliance lead proposes closing the telehealth service, which supports the hospital's growth strategy, because access-logging gaps put its privacy risk above appetite. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Avoid the risk by closing the telehealth service
options.B: Mitigate the risk until it falls within appetite
options.C: Accept the above-appetite risk and record the decision
options.D: Transfer the risk to the platform vendor by contract

questions.key_concept: Avoidance fits only when an activity is not needed for objectives or no treatment can bring its risk within appetite.
questions.pre_read: Note the service's role in the strategy and where its risk sits, then test each response against both.
questions.correct_explanation: Avoidance gives up the activity and its benefit, so it fits when the activity is not needed or no response can bring the risk within appetite. Telehealth supports the growth strategy, and its risk comes from access-logging gaps that controls can close, so the practitioner recommends mitigation down to appetite. Closing the service sacrifices an objective the response is meant to protect. The risk owner then decides.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it removes the exposure. It also gives up a service that supports the growth strategy, when closing the logging gaps could bring the risk within appetite.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the service drives growth. Strategic value alone does not make a risk above appetite acceptable; when controls can close the gap, it argues for treating the risk.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the vendor runs the platform. A contract can share costs, but the hospital still answers to patients and regulators for their privacy.

tips: Eliminate: C keeps a risk that exceeds appetite, and D treats a contract as moving the hospital's privacy accountability to the vendor.
Final two: B beats A because avoidance sacrifices an objective the business needs; when controls can bring risk within appetite, mitigation keeps both the service and the limit.
Exam cue: before choosing avoid, ask whether the activity serves a business objective; if it does, look for the response that treats the risk instead.

questions.subtopic: 3A1 Risk response options. Generative AI replies
questions.question: A bank plans to let a generative AI tool draft replies to customers' loan disputes, and the analyzed risk of wrong advice exceeds appetite. Which response should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Rely on the vendor's contract clause covering losses from wrong replies
options.B: Ban the use of generative AI tools across the bank
options.C: Require a trained staff member to review each draft before sending
options.D: Accept the risk and let staff correct replies after complaints

questions.key_concept: AI risk above appetite is treated with controls such as human review; a vendor clause shifts cost, not accountability.
questions.pre_read: Note where the risk sits against appetite, and trace what happens to one wrong draft under each option.
questions.correct_explanation: The risk exceeds appetite, so it needs treatment. Human review of each draft is a mitigating control placed before the harm occurs: it stops wrong advice from reaching customers and keeps the benefit of the tool. A vendor liability clause is a transfer: it may pay back some losses, but customers still receive wrong advice and the bank still answers for it. The risk owner then accepts what remains.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the vendor built the tool. Contract terms share costs; customers still get wrong advice, and regulators hold the bank accountable.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it removes the AI risk. A bank-wide ban gives up benefits far beyond this one use, when a control aimed at this use may be enough.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because errors can be fixed later. The risk is above appetite, and fixing replies after customers act on them does not prevent the harm.

tips: Eliminate: B avoids far more activity than this risk requires, and D keeps a risk above appetite and relies on repairing harm after it happens.
Final two: C beats A because human review stops wrong advice before it reaches customers; a vendor clause shifts part of the cost and none of the accountability.
Exam cue: for AI risk above appetite, look for a control that checks outputs before they take effect, not a contract that pays afterward.

questions.subtopic: 3A2 Risk and control ownership. Owner for a recovery control
questions.question: A manufacturer's register names the production director as owner of the scheduling-outage risk and the nightly server backup that IT staff run. Who should the risk practitioner propose as the backup's MOST appropriate owner?

options.A: The production director
options.B: The night-shift backup operator
options.C: The risk practitioner
options.D: The IT infrastructure manager

questions.key_concept: The control owner is accountable for a control operating effectively, usually as the manager whose team runs it; the risk owner answers for the risk.
questions.pre_read: Note which role the register already gives the director, and what the backup control needs from its owner.
questions.correct_explanation: A control owner makes the decisions about a control and answers for it being in place and working; the risk owner stays accountable for the risk the control reduces. The production director remains risk owner and relies on the infrastructure manager, whose team runs the backup, to keep it working at the level the director accepted. Naming the director would give the backup an owner with no authority over the team that runs it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because one owner seems simpler. The director has no authority over the IT staff who run backups, so nobody able to fix a failing backup would answer for it.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the operator runs the backup each night. Running a control is not owning it; the owner needs authority over its staffing, tools and fixes.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the practitioner tracks the control. The practitioner validates ownership and reports gaps but does not own or run controls.

tips: Eliminate: B confuses running the backup with owning it, and C makes the practitioner a control owner, when the practitioner validates and reports instead.
Final two: D beats A because the control owner must answer for the backup working, usually as the manager whose team runs it; the director stays risk owner and relies on that control.

Exam cue: risk owner and control owner are different roles; the control owner answers for the control working, usually as the manager whose team runs it, while the business manager owns the risk it reduces.

questions.subtopic: 3A3 Vendor/supply chain risk management. Report scope
questions.question: A university's finance director relies on the student-fees payment provider's independent controls report, tested over a full year, which excludes the subcontractor that processes card refunds. What should the risk analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Ask the director to obtain assurance on the subcontractor
options.B: Rely on the provider's contractual liability for refund errors
options.C: Accept the report's full-year testing as enough assurance
options.D: Advise the director to end the contract and bring refunds in-house

questions.key_concept: An assurance report covers only its stated scope; an excluded fourth party is a gap the business owner closes with assurance of its own.
questions.pre_read: Check what the report covers, and which part of the service it leaves out.
questions.correct_explanation: An assurance report covers only the services and parties in its scope. Refund processing sits with an excluded subcontractor, a fourth party, so the report says nothing about those controls. The analyst first asks the finance director, who owns the vendor risk, to obtain assurance such as the subcontractor's own report, and notes the gap against the vendor risk. A liability clause may recover some costs, but it gives no evidence the refunds are right.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the provider has signed up to cover errors. Liability shares cost after the fact; it gives no evidence that refunds are being processed correctly.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the testing ran for a full year. Period testing covers only what is in scope, and the subcontractor was excluded from it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it would remove the gap. Exit is a large step to advise before anyone has assessed the gap or sought the missing assurance.

tips: Eliminate: C trusts a report for a scope it excludes, and D moves to exit the contract before the gap has been assessed.
Final two: A beats B because the finance director needs evidence the excluded controls work; a liability clause shifts cost but proves nothing about them.
Exam cue: with an assurance report, check its scope and period first; an excluded subcontractor is a gap the service's business owner closes with assurance of its own.

questions.subtopic: 3A4 Issues, findings, exceptions and exemptions management. Deviation request
questions.question: A clinic's imaging system cannot meet the new encryption standard until next year's upgrade; the imaging manager, who owns its risk, asks the risk analyst to approve an exception. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Approve a one-year exception, then assess its risk
options.B: Have the risk owner record an exemption from the standard
options.C: Assess the risk of running the system without encryption
options.D: Have the clinic stop using the system until it complies

questions.key_concept: An exception is a temporary deviation the risk owner approves, with compensating controls and an expiry; the practitioner assesses and advises.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the standard applies to this system, and who may accept the risk of not meeting it.
questions.correct_explanation: The requirement applies but cannot be met for a time, so this is an exception, and granting it accepts risk, which is the risk owner's decision. The analyst first assesses the risk of the gap, then proposes compensating controls, such as restricting image access, for the owner's time-bound approval. The policy owner records the approved exception. An exemption would drop the expiry that forces the upgrade.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the fix date is known. Approving a deviation accepts its risk, a decision for the risk owner, and the risk must be assessed before, not after.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the system cannot comply now. An exemption is a standing exclusion with no end date; this gap ends at next year's upgrade, so a time-bound exception fits.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it closes the gap. Stopping a clinical system before assessing the risk may harm patient care more than the encryption gap does.

tips: Eliminate: A has the analyst accepting risk by approving the deviation, and D halts a clinical system before its risk has been assessed.

Final two: C beats B because the requirement still applies, so the deviation is a time-bound exception the risk owner approves once its risk is assessed; an exemption would remove the deadline to comply.
Exam cue: a temporary gap against a requirement that applies is an exception, with compensating controls, an expiry date and risk-owner approval.

questions.subtopic: 3B1 Control frameworks, types and standards. Weekly change comparison
questions.question: Each Monday, a port operator's IT team compares the previous week's firewall changes with approved change tickets and raises an incident for each mismatch. Which of the following BEST describes this control?

options.A: A preventive control
options.B: A detective control
options.C: A corrective control
options.D: A deterrent control

questions.key_concept: A control that reviews events after they happen is detective, even when it targets unauthorized activity.
questions.pre_read: Notice when the comparison happens relative to the change, and what the team does with a mismatch.
questions.correct_explanation: The comparison happens after changes are already live, so the control finds unapproved changes rather than stopping them: it is detective. Calling it preventive overstates protection, because an unapproved rule could be in place for up to a week. Prevention would need approval enforced before a change can be made. Classifying it correctly lets the residual risk rating reflect that week-long exposure.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it targets unapproved changes. It reviews them after they are live, so it cannot stop them from taking effect.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a mismatch leads to action. The control raises an incident; restoring the settings is a separate corrective step.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because reviews can discourage misconduct. That is a side effect; the control's main function is finding changes that already happened.

tips: Eliminate: C credits the review with restoring settings, which a separate step does, and D names a side effect rather than the control's main function.
Final two: B beats A because the review happens after changes are live; prevention must block a change before it takes effect.
Exam cue: ask when the control acts. Before the event is preventive, after it is detective, and repairing the damage is corrective.

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Control design, selection, implementation and analysis. Recurring billing errors
questions.question: Billing errors at a water utility trace to staff retyping meter readings from handheld devices into the billing system. Which of the following is the MOST effective control for the risk practitioner to recommend?

options.A: A larger team that corrects bills after complaints
options.B: A daily supervisor review of sampled readings
options.C: Quarterly retraining of billing staff on data entry
options.D: Automated transfer of readings from the devices

questions.key_concept: The most effective control addresses the root cause of a risk rather than detecting or correcting its symptoms.
questions.pre_read: Find the step in the process that creates the errors before comparing the controls.
questions.correct_explanation: The root cause is the manual retyping step, so the most effective control removes it: an automated transfer from the devices to billing prevents transcription errors at the source. A supervisor's sample review would catch some errors, but only after they are made and only in the sample, so errors still reach customers. The control owner and risk owner then confirm the cost is proportionate.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because customers get fixes faster. Correcting bills after complaints limits damage but lets each error reach customers first.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because review catches mistakes. It detects some errors after entry, and only in its sample; the retyping that causes them continues.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because people make the errors. Retyping invites mistakes however careful staff are; the process step itself is the cause.

tips: Eliminate: C trains people to work around a flawed step, and A repairs bills only after the error has reached customers.
Final two: D beats B because removing the retyping step fixes the cause; a sample review detects some errors after they are made.
Exam cue: when errors recur from a process step, the BEST control changes or removes that step rather than checking its output.

questions.subtopic: 3A1 Risk response options. Two control options
questions.question: A retailer's card-fraud risk exceeds appetite: control X costs $60,000 a year and brings it within appetite, while control Y costs $250,000 a year and leaves almost none. Which is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Implement control Y alone
options.B: Implement both X and Y together
options.C: Implement control X alone
options.D: Implement neither and accept the risk

questions.key_concept: Choose the response expected to bring risk within appetite at a proportionate cost, not the one that removes the most risk.
questions.pre_read: Work out what each option costs and where it leaves the risk relative to appetite.
questions.correct_explanation: The goal is a target risk within appetite at a cost proportionate to the benefit. Control X reaches appetite for $60,000; control Y spends $190,000 more each year to push the risk below a level the business has already said it can live with. That money is better spent on risks still above appetite. The risk owner makes the final choice, informed by this comparison.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because less risk sounds better. Below appetite, the extra $190,000 a year buys reduction the business does not need, at the expense of other risks.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because layering feels thorough. Combining both costs even more for reduction beyond appetite, so the cost far exceeds the benefit.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because both options cost money. The risk is above appetite, so keeping it unchanged is not an acceptable response.

tips: Eliminate: B stacks controls past what appetite requires, and D keeps a risk that the stem says exceeds appetite.
Final two: C beats A because, once risk is within appetite, extra spending buys reduction the business has not asked for; proportion decides, not maximum reduction.
Exam cue: when two controls both work, prefer the one that meets appetite at the lower total cost, unless a law or contract requires more.

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Control design, selection, implementation and analysis. New review before go-live
questions.question: A risk analyst at a software company is helping the support manager set up a weekly review of bulk customer-data exports. What is MOST important to agree before the review goes live?

options.A: A documented procedure naming who performs the review
options.B: Internal audit's approval of the review design in advance
options.C: The risk owner's acceptance of a lower rating from the first review
options.D: The analyst's sign-off on the first review's results

questions.key_concept: A new control needs a documented procedure, a named performer and an evidence trail, agreed with the control owner before go-live.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the control needs in order to work from what the register will say once it does.
questions.correct_explanation: Before a control goes live, the analyst works with the support manager, as control owner, to document how the review is performed, who performs it and what evidence it leaves. Without that, the review cannot be tested and fails quietly when people change jobs. Recording a lower residual rating is premature: risk counts as reduced only after the review is shown to operate. The risk owner then accepts the new rating.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because audit gives assurance. Internal audit assesses controls independently afterward; approving management's design in advance would weaken that independence.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the owner should accept the new rating. One review shows the control exists, not that it works; the rating changes once operation is shown.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the analyst knows the risk. Signing off its results makes the analyst part of the control; the support team performs it and its manager answers for it.

tips: Eliminate: D makes the analyst part of the control by signing off its results, and B asks internal audit to approve a management control it must later assess independently.
Final two: A beats C because a control needs a documented procedure and a named performer before it can work; the residual rating changes only after it is shown to operate.
Exam cue: before go-live, look for a documented procedure, a named performer and an evidence trail; after go-live, look for proof it operates before lowering the risk.

questions.subtopic: 3B3 Control testing methodologies. Evidence for a daily control
questions.question: A bank's control owner says the daily reconciliation of outgoing payment files has run without a gap this year. Before crediting it in the residual rating, which evidence should the risk analyst rely on MOST?

options.A: A signed statement from the owner confirming daily completion
options.B: Reconciliation records for a sample of days the analyst selects
options.C: Observation of the owner performing today's reconciliation
options.D: The written procedure that describes each reconciliation step

questions.key_concept: For operating effectiveness, evidence across the period that the tester selects beats inquiry and one-time observation.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each piece of evidence would show if the control had been skipped on some days.
questions.correct_explanation: Operating effectiveness needs evidence that the control ran over the period, not just once. Inspecting reconciliation records for days the analyst chooses tests that directly and keeps the selection out of the owner's hands. Watching today's reconciliation shows the control can be done and was done once, while the owner knew they were being observed, so it says little about the other days.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it is formal and signed. It is still inquiry: it records what the owner believes, not evidence that the work was done.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the analyst sees the control first-hand. It covers one day, with the owner aware of being watched, not the whole period.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it shows how the control should work. A procedure supports the design, not whether reconciliations were actually performed.

tips: Eliminate: A is inquiry in written form, and D documents the design rather than showing the control ran.
Final two: B beats C because records for analyst-chosen days cover the period; observation shows one day, while the owner knows they are watched.
Exam cue: for operating effectiveness, prefer evidence across the period that the tester selects, inspects or reperforms over statements or one-time observation.

questions.subtopic: 3C1 Risk action plans. Plan reported complete
questions.question: A telecom's network manager reports that the action plan to require multifactor sign-in for remote access is complete. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Lower the residual risk rating and close the action plan
options.B: Obtain evidence that the control is enforced for remote users
options.C: Report the completed plan to the risk owner and the risk committee
options.D: Accept the manager's signed statement as completion evidence

questions.key_concept: The practitioner validates with evidence that an action plan was carried out before re-rating the risk or reporting it complete.
questions.pre_read: Notice who says the plan is complete, and what evidence exists so far.
questions.correct_explanation: A plan reported complete is not yet proven complete. The practitioner first obtains evidence, such as sign-in configuration reports or test results, that multifactor sign-in is enforced for remote users. Only then can the residual risk be re-rated and progress reported. Reporting completion to the owner and committee first would pass on an unverified claim that could lead them to stop watching the risk.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the plan says done. Lowering the rating on the manager's word could understate a risk whose control may not be enforced.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because reporting progress is part of the job. Reporting before validation passes an unverified claim to the people who decide.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a signed statement looks formal. It is still the manager's own claim; completion needs evidence such as configuration reports or test results.

tips: Eliminate: A re-rates the risk on a status report, and D treats the manager's own claim as proof of completion.
Final two: B beats C because the practitioner validates completion before reporting it; otherwise the owner and committee decide on an unverified claim.
Exam cue: done is a claim until evidence shows the control is in place and working; validate before you re-rate or report.

questions.subtopic: 3C2 Data collection, aggregation, analysis and validation. Mixed rating scales
questions.question: An enterprise risk analyst at a retail group is combining unit risk registers: two units score risks from 1 to 5, and one uses high, medium and low. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Add each unit's scores together to rank the group's risks
options.B: Average the scores to weight each unit equally
options.C: Map the ratings onto one common scale and set of criteria
options.D: List each unit's top risks as rated in one combined table

questions.key_concept: Risk ratings from different scales must be normalized to common criteria before they are aggregated or compared.
questions.pre_read: Look at how each unit rates its risks before deciding how to combine them.
questions.correct_explanation: Ratings on different scales cannot be compared, added or averaged, so the first step is normalizing them onto the group's common scale and criteria, for example mapping high, medium and low to numbers. Only then can duplicates be merged and risks ranked across units. Listing each unit's top risks as rated keeps them visible, but leaves senior management comparing a 4 with a high.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because totals look decisive. Adding scores from different scales gives numbers with no shared meaning and can bury a severe single risk.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it seems fair to every unit. Averaging still mixes scales and pulls a critical risk toward the middle.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because nothing is lost. Without a common scale, readers cannot compare risks across units or rank them.

tips: Eliminate: A and B do arithmetic on ratings from different scales, which buries severe risks and gives totals with no common meaning.
Final two: C beats D because comparison needs common criteria first; a list kept on each unit's own scale keeps the risks visible but impossible to rank.
Exam cue: before aggregating risk data, normalize it; one scale and one set of criteria come before any ranking, totaling or reporting.

questions.subtopic: 3C3 Risk and control metrics. Indicator for a ransomware risk
questions.question: Which of the following should a risk analyst propose as the BEST key risk indicator for the risk of ransomware halting a food manufacturer's production lines?

options.A: Ransomware incidents recorded in the past year
options.B: Awareness sessions delivered each quarter
options.C: Average recovery time after past outages
options.D: VPN accounts without multifactor sign-in

questions.key_concept: The best key risk indicator is relevant to the scenario and leading: it tracks a driver of the risk, not past incidents.
questions.pre_read: For each metric, ask what it would tell the owner about this particular risk, and when.
questions.correct_explanation: A good KRI is relevant to the risk scenario, measurable and leading: it moves before the event. VPN accounts without multifactor sign-in are a known way in for ransomware, so a rising count warns that exposure is building. A count of past incidents is relevant but lagging. The VPN measure could also serve as a KCI for access control; here it is a KRI because it tracks exposure in the ransomware scenario.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it measures ransomware directly. Incidents are a lagging outcome; by the time the count goes up, the harm has occurred.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because awareness reduces some attacks. It counts activity delivered, a performance measure, not exposure to this risk.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because recovery speed shapes how long production stops. It measures past recovery performance, a lagging measure, not whether ransomware exposure is building now.

tips: Eliminate: B counts training delivered and C measures recovery after past outages; both describe performance, not exposure building in the ransomware scenario.
Final two: D beats A because a KRI should warn before the event; VPN accounts without multifactor sign-in are a leading driver, while incidents are a lagging outcome.
Exam cue: the BEST KRI is relevant, measurable and leading; prefer a driver of the risk over a count of past losses or incidents.

questions.subtopic: 3C3 Risk and control metrics. Setting a red threshold
questions.question: An airline's IT team proposes an 8% red threshold, taken from an industry survey, for the KRI on unpatched booking servers; the commercial director owns the outage risk. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Derive the red threshold from the airline's approved outage tolerance
options.B: Keep the 8% survey figure as an accepted industry benchmark
options.C: Have IT set the tolerance at the patch level staff can sustain
options.D: Replace the KRI with the director's monthly outage count

questions.key_concept: KRI thresholds come from the organization's approved tolerance, agreed with the risk owner; industry figures are context, not limits.
questions.pre_read: Before judging the 8% figure, ask what a red threshold is meant to signal, and to whom.
questions.correct_explanation: A red threshold should mark the point where the risk passes the outage tolerance senior management approved, so it is derived from that tolerance and agreed with the commercial director as risk owner. A survey figure reflects other airlines' appetite, exposure and patch practices; it is useful context but says nothing about this business's limit. The practitioner proposes the derivation, and the owner agrees the threshold.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because benchmarks feel objective. Other firms' figures reflect their own appetite and exposure, not this airline's tolerance for booking outages.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because IT knows what is achievable. Letting the control team set its own limit measures workload, not the level of risk the business will tolerate.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because outages are what the director cares about. An outage count is lagging; unpatched servers are the leading driver the KRI is meant to watch.

tips: Eliminate: C lets the team running the control set its own limit, and D swaps a leading driver for a lagging count of outages.
Final two: A beats B because a threshold must reflect this organization's approved tolerance, agreed with the risk owner; a survey figure is context, not a limit.
Exam cue: when a threshold comes from a benchmark, a vendor default or team capacity, look for the option that ties it to the organization's own tolerance.

questions.subtopic: 3C3 Risk and control metrics. Pricing model indicator
questions.question: Which of the following should a risk practitioner propose as the BEST early warning indicator for a machine-learning model that prices an insurer's home policies?

options.A: Accuracy measured at the model's last validation
options.B: Customer complaints about prices each quarter
options.C: Weekly shift in input data from the training baseline
options.D: Share of underwriters trained to use the model

questions.key_concept: AI model risk needs leading production indicators, such as input drift, not only lagging signals such as complaints.
questions.pre_read: Ask which indicator would move first if the model began to go wrong.
questions.correct_explanation: Drift in the input data is an early sign that pricing errors may follow, so tracking it weekly gives the owner time to retrain or review the model. Complaints are relevant but lagging: they arrive after mispriced policies reach customers, and many affected customers never complain. A single accuracy figure from the last validation cannot show any change in production.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because accuracy is the core quality measure. Measured once at validation, it cannot show whether performance has changed since deployment.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because complaints reflect real harm. They lag behind the errors, arrive quarterly and miss customers who never complain.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because training reduces misuse. It measures an activity, a performance measure, not whether the model itself is degrading.

tips: Eliminate: A is a one-time snapshot that cannot show change in production, and D measures training activity rather than the model's behavior.
Final two: C beats B because input drift is an early sign of pricing errors; complaints arrive after customers are harmed.
Exam cue: for AI models, early warning comes from production monitoring of drift and error trends; complaints and incidents confirm harm after it happens.

questions.subtopic: 3C4 Risk and control monitoring techniques. Unread alerts
questions.question: A law firm's monitoring tool sends alerts to a shared inbox when laptop antivirus is disabled, and the risk analyst finds the majority of them unread. What should the analyst recommend as MOST important?

options.A: Add a second monitoring tool to widen laptop coverage
options.B: Name an owner to check the shared inbox once a month
options.C: Flag the alerts as high priority in the shared inbox
options.D: Route each alert type to a responder with a deadline

questions.key_concept: Automated monitoring reduces risk only when each alert reaches a named responder who acts within a set time.
questions.pre_read: Ask what happens after an alert is sent, and who is expected to act on it.
questions.correct_explanation: Monitoring reduces risk only when someone acts on what it finds. Alerts sent to a shared inbox have no owner, so disabled antivirus goes unanswered. Routing each alert type to a named responder with a response deadline, tracked to closure, turns detection into response. A monthly inbox check names an owner but leaves laptops unprotected for weeks between checks, so it is the runner-up.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because broader coverage sounds safer. More alerts into an unread inbox add volume without adding any response.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it names an owner. A monthly check leaves disabled antivirus unanswered for weeks; the response time must match how fast the exposure grows.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because urgent flags draw the eye. A flag gives no one the duty to act; alerts in an unowned inbox stay unread however they are marked.

tips: Eliminate: A adds alerts to a queue nobody works, and C makes unowned alerts louder without giving anyone the duty to act.
Final two: D beats B because each alert needs a named responder acting within a set time; a monthly inbox check names an owner but leaves exposure open for weeks.
Exam cue: when monitoring exists but nothing happens, the fix is ownership and a response time, not more alerts or louder ones.

questions.question: Which of the following should a risk analyst consider MOST appropriate for a bank's quarterly IT risk report to the board risk committee?

options.A: Risks beyond appetite, with trend and decisions needed
options.B: A heat map plotting the full risk register against appetite
options.C: Open vulnerabilities by system, with their severity ratings

questions.key_concept: Board risk reporting shows the profile against appetite, trends and the decisions needed, not operational detail.
questions.pre_read: Think about which decisions the board makes, then pick the content that supports them.
questions.correct_explanation: The board sets appetite and makes the major risk decisions, so its report should show where the profile sits against appetite, which way key risks are moving and what it is being asked to decide. wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because control results show assurance. Test-by-test detail suits risk and control owners; the board needs the overall effect against appetite.

tips: Eliminate: C and D give the board operational detail that suits the teams and owners who act on it, not the body that sets appetite.
Final two: A beats B because the board needs risks against appetite, their trend and the decision asked of it; a full heat map shows position only.

questions.subtopic: 3C6 Monitoring and reporting of emerging risks. Rules under consultation
questions.question: A pharmacy chain is piloting an AI tool for patient reminder messages when the risk analyst learns that regulators are consulting on rules for AI in patient communications. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Ask the owner to pause the pilot until rules are final
options.B: Record it as an emerging risk in the register
options.C: Wait for the final rules before assessing the impact
options.D: Rate the regulatory risk as critical in the register

questions.key_concept: Emerging risks are recorded early with stated uncertainty, an owner and a review date, then refined as evidence grows.
questions.pre_read: Notice how certain the new rules are, and what each option does with that uncertainty.
questions.correct_explanation: A consultation is an early signal: the rules may change the pilot's obligations, but their content and timing are uncertain. The analyst records it in the register as an emerging risk, with its uncertainty stated, a business owner and a short review date, then refines it as the rules take shape. Pausing the pilot now gives up its benefit on a guess about rules that do not yet exist.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it avoids breaking future rules. Pausing gives up the pilot's benefit before anyone knows what the rules will require.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the rules are not final. Waiting leaves no time to prepare; emerging risks are recorded early and refined as they develop.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it gets attention. Overstating certainty misdirects budget and damages trust; the rating should reflect what is actually known.

tips: Eliminate: C waits until the rules are final, leaving no time to prepare, and D overstates a risk whose details are still unknown.
Final two: B beats A because the rules are still uncertain; recording the emerging risk with an owner keeps the pilot's benefit while preparing for whatever the rules require.
Exam cue: for an emerging risk, record it early with its uncertainty, an owner and a review date; neither dismiss it nor treat it as certain.

questions.subtopic: 3A1 Risk response options. Recording an acceptance
questions.question: A risk owner at a regional newspaper group has formally accepted a residual risk that sits within appetite. Which of the following is MOST important to record with the acceptance?

options.A: Internal audit's agreement with the decision
options.B: The risk practitioner's approval of the rationale
options.C: A date for reviewing the acceptance
options.D: A note closing the risk in the register

questions.key_concept: Risk acceptance is a dated, owned decision that is reviewed later; the accepted risk stays in the register and is monitored.
questions.pre_read: Ask what happens to an accepted risk after the decision is signed.
questions.correct_explanation: Acceptance is a decision made at a point in time, and conditions change. A review date makes the risk owner confirm later that the risk still fits appetite, while the risk stays in the register under monitoring. A closing note is the tempting alternative: accepted risk is still the organization's risk, so removing it from the register would leave it unwatched until it causes a loss.

wrong_explanations.A: Internal audit gives independent assurance on the process later. Its agreement is not needed for an owner's acceptance within appetite, and seeking it blurs the lines of defense.
wrong_explanations.B: The practitioner documents and advises on the acceptance but does not approve it; the decision and its rationale belong to the risk owner.
wrong_explanations.D: Accepted risk remains the organization's exposure. It stays in the register and is monitored, because its rating can drift above tolerance as conditions change.

tips: Eliminate: A adds an assurance step the decision does not need, and B gives the practitioner an approval that belongs to the risk owner.
Final two: C beats D because an accepted risk stays in the register under monitoring; a review date makes the owner look again when conditions change.
Exam cue: acceptance is not closure. An accepted risk stays recorded, owned and monitored, with a date to revisit the decision.

questions.subtopic: 3A2 Risk and control ownership. Validating a risk owner
questions.question: Which of the following BEST shows a risk practitioner that the named owner of a business risk is performing the role?

options.A: Response decisions the owner has recorded and signed
options.B: The owner's name recorded against the risk in the register
options.C: The owner's attendance at annual risk training
options.D: The owner's senior grade on the organization chart

questions.key_concept: Risk ownership is validated by evidence that the owner makes and records decisions on the risk, not by an assignment in the register.
questions.pre_read: Ask what record could only exist if the owner were really doing the job.
questions.correct_explanation: Ownership is shown by the role being exercised: response choices, acceptances and plan approvals the owner has recorded and signed. These show the person is making the decisions they are accountable for. A name in the register is the closest alternative: it shows who was assigned, not whether that person has ever decided anything about the risk.

wrong_explanations.B: A register entry shows the assignment. It cannot show that the owner reviews the risk, chooses responses or accepts what remains.
wrong_explanations.C: Training builds awareness of the role. Attending a course does not show the owner has made any decision about this risk.
wrong_explanations.D: Seniority helps an owner fund and decide, but grade alone does not show the role is being carried out.

tips: Eliminate: C shows awareness rather than decisions, and D shows authority on paper with no sign it is used.
Final two: A beats B because validating ownership needs evidence of decisions taken; a name in the register only records who was assigned.
Exam cue: to validate a role, look for the outputs of the role, such as signed decisions, not the label that assigns it.

questions.subtopic: 3A2 Risk and control ownership. Owner of a double-booking risk
questions.question: A hotel group's register names its reservations IT lead as owner of the peak-season double-booking risk, but the distribution director runs bookings and controls the treatment's funds. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Keep the IT lead as owner, copying the distribution director
options.B: Name the IT lead and the director as joint owners
options.C: Have the IT lead accept the risk until funds are approved
options.D: Propose the distribution director as the risk's owner

questions.key_concept: A risk is owned by one business manager with authority over the affected objective and the budget for its treatment.
questions.pre_read: Compare the role the register names with the roles the risk's outcome and treatment depend on.
questions.correct_explanation: A risk owner needs authority over the objective and the budget the response depends on. The distribution director runs the bookings the risk affects and controls the funds, so the director should own it, with the IT lead supporting as a control owner. Joint ownership is the closest alternative: it looks inclusive, but it splits accountability so that each owner can wait for the other to act.

wrong_explanations.A: Copying the director keeps them informed, but the owner of record still cannot fund the treatment, so the response stalls.
wrong_explanations.B: Two owners blur accountability. When funding or acceptance is needed, each can defer to the other and nobody decides.
wrong_explanations.C: An owner without budget authority cannot accept the risk on the business's behalf, and waiting for funds leaves the exposure untreated.

tips: Eliminate: A leaves ownership with someone who cannot fund the response, and C has that person accept a risk beyond their authority.
Final two: D beats B because one named owner, accountable for bookings and holding the budget, can decide; joint owners can each defer to the other.
Exam cue: the risk owner is the manager whose objective and budget the risk affects; IT supports as control owner.

questions.subtopic: 3A1 Risk response options. Acceptance above delegated authority
questions.question: A logistics firm's policy lets department heads accept residual risks rated up to medium, and the warehouse head has signed acceptance of a residual risk rated high. What is the risk practitioner's BEST action?

options.A: File the signed acceptance in the register as approved
options.B: Refer the acceptance to the executive authorized for high risks
options.C: Lower the risk's rating to medium to match the signer's authority
options.D: Co-sign the acceptance on behalf of the risk function

questions.key_concept: Risk acceptance must come from someone whose delegated authority covers the rating; an acceptance beyond it is elevated.
questions.pre_read: Compare the rating the head may accept with the rating of this risk.
questions.correct_explanation: Acceptance authority is delegated by rating, so a high residual risk must be accepted by someone who holds that authority. The practitioner refers the decision upward, with the analysis, rather than filing an acceptance the signer could not give. Filing it is the closest alternative: the signature looks formal, but it records a decision outside policy and leaves the firm holding a high risk nobody with authority agreed to.

wrong_explanations.A: A signature outside delegated authority is not a valid acceptance. Filing it would record a high risk as approved when no one with that authority has agreed.
wrong_explanations.C: The rating comes from the analysis, not from who signed. Lowering it to fit the signer's authority would misstate the exposure.
wrong_explanations.D: The risk function advises and records; it does not accept risk. Its co-signature cannot supply authority the warehouse head lacks.

tips: Eliminate: C changes the analysis to suit the approver, and D has the risk function take part in an acceptance decision.
Final two: B beats A because an acceptance beyond the signer's delegated limit is not valid; it goes to the level that holds that authority.
Exam cue: when a decision exceeds someone's authority, elevate it to the level that holds the authority; never resize the risk to fit.

questions.subtopic: 3A3 Vendor/supply chain risk management. Refused right to audit
questions.question: At renewal, the cloud provider hosting a university's student-records system, rated critical in its vendor inventory, says it no longer grants any customer a right to audit. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Require yearly independent assurance reports on the service
options.B: Accept the renewal as offered and note the refusal on the file
options.C: Rely on the provider's yearly security questionnaire
options.D: End the relationship and move the system to a new provider

questions.key_concept: When a critical vendor refuses a right to audit, independent assurance reports written into the contract give the evidence the business still needs.
questions.pre_read: Notice how critical the service is and what the provider's refusal takes away.
questions.correct_explanation: The university still answers for its student records, so it needs reliable assurance about the provider's controls. When a provider grants no customer audits, independent assurance reports covering the hosting service, written into the contract, are the usual substitute. The provider's own questionnaire is the closest alternative: it is easy to obtain, but self-reported answers give weak assurance for a critical service.

wrong_explanations.B: Noting the refusal records the gap but leaves the university with no assurance about a critical service it still answers for.
wrong_explanations.C: A questionnaire is the provider describing itself. It suits low-risk vendors, not a critical service holding students' personal records.
wrong_explanations.D: Leaving is an avoidance response chosen before other assurance routes are tried, and it carries its own migration risk.

tips: Eliminate: B accepts a gap in assurance for a critical service, and D chooses exit before cheaper assurance routes are tried.
Final two: A beats C because independent assurance is reliable evidence for a critical vendor; a self-completed questionnaire is the provider's own claim.
Exam cue: match assurance to criticality; critical vendors need independent evidence, written into the contract.

questions.subtopic: 3A3 Vendor/supply chain risk management. Clean assurance report
questions.question: A city council's payroll provider gives it a SOC 2 Type 2 report covering the payroll service for the past 12 months, with no exceptions. What should the risk practitioner review MOST closely?

options.A: The provider's service level results for the same period
options.B: The financial statements the provider filed for the year
options.C: The customer controls the report expects the council to run
options.D: The test steps the service auditor applied to each control

questions.key_concept: A vendor's assurance report relies on complementary customer controls; the customer must run them for the report's assurance to hold.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a clean SOC 2 Type 2 report proves for the council, and what it leaves open.
questions.correct_explanation: A clean report covers the provider's side of the controls, and it usually assumes customers run their own complementary controls, such as reviewing who holds payroll administrator access. If the council does not run them, the assurance does not hold for the council. The auditor's test steps are the closest alternative: the clean opinion already rests on them, while the council's own duties are what the report cannot test.

wrong_explanations.A: Service level results show performance against targets, such as availability, not whether the security controls the council depends on are designed and operating.
wrong_explanations.B: Financial health matters for continuity, but it says nothing about whether payroll data is protected under this report.
wrong_explanations.D: The service auditor's testing supports the clean opinion. Re-examining it adds little, while the controls the council must run itself are untested by anyone.

tips: Eliminate: A measures service performance, and B measures financial health; neither shows whether the controls protecting payroll data work.
Final two: C beats D because the clean opinion already covers the auditor's testing; the report cannot cover the controls it expects the council to run.
Exam cue: an assurance report covers the vendor's side only; check the customer controls it assumes before relying on it.

questions.subtopic: 3A3 Vendor/supply chain risk management. AI vendor service credits
questions.question: An insurer's vendor AI tool sets payouts from damage photos, with service credits if accuracy falls below 97%, and the claims director wants to stop the insurer's sampling. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Rely on the vendor's service credits for accuracy shortfalls
options.B: Keep the insurer's own sampling of the tool's payouts
options.C: Replace the sampling with the vendor's monthly accuracy report
options.D: Suspend the AI tool until its accuracy is independently proven

questions.key_concept: An AI vendor's service credits shift some financial loss, not accountability; the business keeps monitoring the outputs it relies on.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the service credit pays for, and what it does not catch.
questions.correct_explanation: Service credits refund part of the fee when accuracy slips; they neither detect a wrong payout nor repair the harm to a customer. The insurer stays accountable for each payout, so it keeps its own sampling of outputs. The vendor's accuracy report is the closest alternative: it helps, but it is the vendor measuring itself, on its own definitions, not the insurer checking the payouts it makes.

wrong_explanations.A: Credits compensate the insurer financially. They do not find wrong payouts or reduce the harm to customers and regulators, which stays with the insurer.
wrong_explanations.C: A vendor's report is useful input, but it is self-measured and may not reflect the insurer's own claims and customers.
wrong_explanations.D: Suspending the tool is avoidance with no sign of failure. Sampling already manages the risk while the tool delivers its benefit.

tips: Eliminate: A treats a financial remedy as a control, and D drops the tool's benefit with no sign that it is failing.
Final two: B beats C because the insurer stays accountable for each payout and needs its own check; the vendor's report is the vendor measuring itself.
Exam cue: contracts move money, not accountability; keep monitoring the AI outputs your business relies on.

questions.subtopic: 3A4 Issues, findings, exceptions and exemptions management. Requirement that cannot apply
questions.question: A city library's self-service catalog kiosks have no user accounts, so its password standard cannot apply to them. Which of the following should the risk practitioner recommend as MOST appropriate?

options.A: An exception the risk owner approves for 90 days
options.B: An exemption the risk owner approves and reviews
options.C: An exception the IT manager approves for 90 days
options.D: An exemption the risk practitioner approves and files

questions.key_concept: An exemption covers a requirement that cannot apply and is reviewed periodically; an exception is temporary. The risk owner approves both.
questions.pre_read: Read why the standard is not met before choosing how the deviation is handled.
questions.correct_explanation: An exemption fits a requirement that does not or cannot apply, as with kiosks that have no accounts. The risk owner approves it after the practitioner assesses the risk, and it is reviewed periodically in case the kiosks change. A 90-day exception approved by the risk owner is the closest alternative: exceptions are temporary deviations with a plan to comply, but here there is nothing to comply toward.

wrong_explanations.A: An exception assumes the kiosks will later meet the standard. With no accounts there is no plan to comply, so an expiry date only forces repeated renewals.
wrong_explanations.C: The IT manager runs the kiosks' technology but does not own the library's risk, and an exception assumes the kiosks will later meet the standard, which they cannot.
wrong_explanations.D: The practitioner assesses the risk and records the deviation but does not approve it; approval belongs to the risk owner.

tips: Eliminate: C has the IT manager, not the risk owner, approve a temporary deviation, and D has the practitioner approve a deviation the risk owner must approve.
Final two: B beats A because the standard cannot apply to these kiosks; an exemption is reviewed periodically, while an exception expires pending compliance.

Exam cue: on CRISC items, a requirement that can never apply is usually handled as a reviewed exemption, and a temporary shortfall as an exception with a date to comply; the risk owner approves either.

questions.subtopic: 3A4 Issues, findings, exceptions and exemptions management. Remediation date missed twice
questions.question: An airline's fix for an audit finding on shared administrator accounts has missed two due dates, and the IT manager who owns the action proposes a third date. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Record the action owner's third date in the tracker
options.B: Close the finding and log a new one with the new date
options.C: Ask the IT manager to accept the risk until the new date
options.D: Escalate the repeated slippage to the risk owner

questions.key_concept: Repeatedly overdue remediation is escalated to the risk owner, who decides on resources, plan changes or the risk itself.
questions.pre_read: Count how many dates have already passed, and ask who can change the outcome.
questions.correct_explanation: Two missed dates show the plan is not working, and the exposure from shared administrator accounts stays open while it slips. The practitioner escalates to the risk owner, who can add resources, change the plan or decide on the risk. Recording a third date is the closest alternative: tracking matters, but quietly accepting each new date lets an overdue finding drift with no accountable person deciding.

wrong_explanations.A: Updating the tracker keeps the record current, but accepting a third date without escalation lets the slippage continue unchallenged.
wrong_explanations.B: Closing and reopening a finding hides its age and history, which are what show the risk owner the fix is slipping.
wrong_explanations.C: The IT manager owns the action, not the risk, so they cannot accept the exposure on the business's behalf.

tips: Eliminate: B resets the finding's history, and C has the action owner accept a risk that belongs to the risk owner.
Final two: D beats A because repeated slippage is a trigger to escalate; recording a third date tracks the delay without anyone deciding about it.
Exam cue: overdue actions go to the risk owner, and past agreed limits to senior management; the tracker records, it does not decide.

questions.subtopic: 3A4 Issues, findings, exceptions and exemptions management. Many exceptions on one asset
questions.question: At a manufacturer, 20 department heads have each approved a low-rated exception letting their contractors use the same legacy VPN gateway without multifactor sign-in. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Assess the combined risk of the exceptions on the gateway
options.B: Ask each department head to assess their own exception again
options.C: Have IT revoke the exceptions and enforce multifactor sign-in
options.D: List the gateway exceptions in a summary for the risk committee

questions.key_concept: Exceptions are tracked in aggregate, because many low-rated deviations on one asset can add up to a risk above appetite.
questions.pre_read: Look at what the exceptions have in common, not at each rating alone.
questions.correct_explanation: Each exception was rated alone, but together they open one gateway to 20 departments' contractors without multifactor sign-in. The practitioner first assesses the combined exposure against appetite, then takes the result to the owners who must decide. Asking each head to reassess is the closest alternative: it repeats the one-at-a-time view that produced the low ratings and still misses the aggregate risk.

wrong_explanations.B: Each head sees only their own contractors. Assessing each exception again, one by one, repeats the view that rated each one low.
wrong_explanations.C: Revoking approved exceptions is a response chosen before the combined risk is known, and the practitioner does not overturn owners' approvals.
wrong_explanations.D: A summary makes the gateway exceptions visible, but without an assessment the committee sees 20 low risks instead of one larger exposure.

tips: Eliminate: C acts before the combined risk is analyzed and overrides the owners, and D reports a list with no assessment behind it.
Final two: A beats B because the exposure comes from the exceptions together; assessing each one again alone repeats the view that missed it.
Exam cue: deviations are rated one at a time but can add up; look at them in aggregate before deciding they are low.

questions.subtopic: 3B1 Control frameworks, types and standards. Supervisor check on a logging gap
questions.question: A port's crane-scheduling system cannot record who changes a schedule, so IT added a daily supervisor check of changes and asks to close the gap in the register. What is the risk practitioner's BEST response?

options.A: Close the gap, recording the daily check as its permanent fix
options.B: Keep the gap open, with the check as a compensating control
options.C: Close the gap once the check has run well for a month
options.D: Record the gap as an accepted risk owned by the IT manager

questions.key_concept: A compensating control reduces risk while a weakness exists; the gap stays recorded and reviewed until it is fixed or the owner decides.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the new check removes the weakness or only reduces its effect.
questions.correct_explanation: A compensating control reduces the risk while the weakness exists, but it does not remove it: the system still cannot show who changed a schedule. The gap stays recorded, with the daily check credited as compensating and reviewed, until the system is fixed or the risk owner decides on it. Closing after a month is the closest alternative: evidence that the check works justifies crediting it, not closing the gap.

wrong_explanations.A: The check finds unexpected changes after the fact; it does not give user-level accountability. Treating it as permanent hides a weakness that still exists.
wrong_explanations.C: A month of evidence shows the check operates, which justifies crediting it in the rating. It does not make the system record who made a change.
wrong_explanations.D: The IT manager runs the system but does not own the business risk, so cannot accept it on the port's behalf.

tips: Eliminate: D has the IT manager accept a business risk, and A treats an after-the-fact check as a permanent fix.
Final two: B beats C because evidence that the check works earns it credit in the rating; it does not make the system record who changed a schedule.
Exam cue: a compensating control covers a gap for now; the gap stays recorded and reviewed until it is fixed or the owner decides.

questions.subtopic: 3B1 Control frameworks, types and standards. Detection after the loss
questions.question: A broker's only control over changes to clients' payout bank details is a weekly report the operations manager reviews, and the fraud risk exceeds appetite. Which addition should the risk practitioner recommend as MOST important?

options.A: A call-back to the client before a change takes effect
options.B: The same change report run daily by the manager
options.C: A second reviewer for the weekly change report
options.D: A yearly staff reminder on handling client changes

questions.key_concept: A layered set mixes control functions; when detection comes only after the loss, a preventive control is the most important addition.
questions.pre_read: Ask when the existing control acts: before or after the money moves.
questions.correct_explanation: The only control detects a fraudulent change days after payouts may already have gone to a criminal's account. Adding a preventive step, such as calling the client on a known number before a change takes effect, stops the fraud before money moves. Running the report daily is the closest alternative: faster detection narrows the window, but it still finds the change after the payout risk has arisen.

wrong_explanations.B: Daily review shortens the window, but it still finds a fraudulent change after it has taken effect and payouts may have gone.
wrong_explanations.C: A second reviewer may catch more on the report, but still up to a week after the change, when payouts may already be lost.
wrong_explanations.D: A reminder supports the procedure but does not stop a criminal who has taken over a client's account from changing the bank details.

tips: Eliminate: C adds a reviewer to the same late report, and D relies on a reminder that cannot stop an outsider's change.
Final two: A beats B because prevention stops the fraudulent change before money moves; a faster report still finds it afterward.
Exam cue: when the only control detects after the loss, look for a preventive layer that stops the event first.

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Control design, selection, implementation and analysis. Defining the desired state
questions.question: Which of the following is the BEST basis for the desired state in a risk practitioner's control gap analysis?

options.A: The controls peers use to stay within their own appetite
options.B: The full control catalog of the chosen framework
options.C: The control level needed to keep risk within appetite
options.D: The controls that IT can deliver within this year's budget

questions.key_concept: The desired state in a control gap analysis is the control level needed to bring risk within appetite and meet obligations.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each option would measure the gaps against.
questions.correct_explanation: The desired state should come from what the business has decided it will tolerate: the controls needed to bring each risk within this organization's appetite, along with any legal or contractual requirement. Peer practice is the closest alternative: it is useful context, but peers set their controls against their own risks, objectives and appetite, so copying them can over- or under-protect this organization.

wrong_explanations.A: Peer controls are set to stay within the peers' own appetite and risks, which may differ from this organization's, so copying them can over- or under-protect it.
wrong_explanations.B: A catalog is a menu to tailor from. Taking all of it as the target overspends on risks that matter little here.
wrong_explanations.D: Budget shapes the plan to close gaps, not the target itself. Setting the target at what IT can afford hides the gaps that matter.

tips: Eliminate: B treats a framework catalog as a checklist, and D lets this year's budget set the target in place of the risk.
Final two: C beats A because the target must reflect this organization's appetite; a peer's appetite is input at most, not the limit this business set.
Exam cue: in a gap analysis, the desired state comes from appetite and obligations; frameworks and peers inform it, budgets schedule it.

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Control design, selection, implementation and analysis. Ordering the gaps
questions.question: A gap analysis at a freight railway lists 14 control gaps, and the CIO wants to close the nine quickest first to show the board progress. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Close the quick gaps first, then plan the rest
options.B: Close the gaps in the order the framework lists them
options.C: Let each control owner set the order for their gaps
options.D: Rank the gaps by the risk each one leaves open

questions.key_concept: Control gaps are ranked by the risk each leaves open, so the largest exposure is funded and fixed first.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the CIO's ordering is designed to show.
questions.correct_explanation: Gaps should be closed in the order of the exposure they leave, so the largest risks to the railway's objectives get resources first; quick fixes can still be scheduled where they fit. Closing the quick gaps first is the closest alternative: it shows progress, but the board would hear that things are improving while the gaps that matter most stay open.

wrong_explanations.A: Quick wins show activity, but they may leave the largest exposures untouched while progress looks good.
wrong_explanations.B: A framework's order reflects how the catalog is arranged, not where this organization's risk is greatest.
wrong_explanations.C: Each owner sees only their own gaps, so the order would follow local preference instead of enterprise exposure.

tips: Eliminate: B follows the catalog's layout, and C lets each owner set an order with no view of enterprise exposure.
Final two: D beats A because resources go first to the gaps that leave the most risk open; quick wins can fit around that order.
Exam cue: prioritize remediation by the risk left open, not by ease, catalog order or local preference.

questions.subtopic: 3B3 Control testing methodologies. One maturity target for all controls
questions.question: To cut costs, a payments processor's IT director proposes one maturity target, level 2 on a 0 to 5 scale, for all IT controls, including card settlement controls. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Adopt level 2 as the common target for IT controls
options.B: Raise the targets for IT controls to the top level
options.C: Set each control's target by the risk it addresses
options.D: Drop maturity targets and rely on control testing

questions.key_concept: Target control maturity is set by the risk each control addresses, agreed with the risk owner, not as one level for every control.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the single target would mean for the highest-risk controls.
questions.correct_explanation: Maturity targets should follow risk: controls protecting card settlement need repeatable, measured practice, while low-risk controls can sit lower. The practitioner proposes targets set with each risk owner by the risk a control addresses, which spends where it matters. Dropping targets for testing is the closest alternative: testing shows a control works today, but maturity shows whether it will keep working.

wrong_explanations.A: One low target saves money on minor controls but under-protects the controls behind the processor's highest risks.
wrong_explanations.B: Top-level maturity everywhere costs far more than lower-risk controls justify; for most of them the cost would exceed the benefit.
wrong_explanations.D: Testing and maturity answer different questions. A control can pass this year's test yet depend on habits that will not last.

tips: Eliminate: A sets one low bar for high and low risks alike, and B pays for top maturity where the risk does not justify it.
Final two: C beats D because testing shows a control works now, while risk-based maturity targets show where it must keep working reliably.
Exam cue: maturity targets are set by risk, neither as high as possible nor as cheap as possible.

questions.subtopic: 3B3 Control testing methodologies. Failures found in a sample
questions.question: Testing a sample of 25 days of a water utility's daily backup check, the risk analyst finds no record for 2 days. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Rate the control ineffective and raise an issue
options.B: Replace the two days with two other sampled days
options.C: Report the control as 92% effective to its owner
options.D: Find out why the check was missed on those two days

questions.key_concept: Failures found in a control test sample are investigated for their cause before the tester concludes whether the control can be relied on.
questions.pre_read: Ask what you would need to know before calling the control effective or not.
questions.correct_explanation: A failure in a sample must be understood before the control is judged. The cause shows whether these were one-off lapses with the backups still checked another way, or a breakdown that undermines reliance on the control. Rating it ineffective now is the closest alternative: it may prove right, but concluding before knowing the cause can misstate the control and the risk.

wrong_explanations.A: The two gaps may lead to that rating, but deciding before the cause is known can misstate the control either way.
wrong_explanations.B: Swapping out failed items hides the result. Failures in a sample are evaluated, not replaced.
wrong_explanations.C: A percentage from a small sample says nothing about why the check was missed or whether it can be relied on.

tips: Eliminate: B removes failures from the sample, and C turns two misses into a pass rate without knowing their cause.
Final two: D beats A because the cause decides whether the control can still be relied on; a rating made before knowing it may be wrong.
Exam cue: in control testing, evaluate each failed sample item's cause before concluding on the control.

questions.subtopic: 3B3 Control testing methodologies. Reconciliation run by one clerk
questions.question: A distributor's monthly supplier-file reconciliation passed every sampled month, but only one clerk knows how to run it and nothing is written down. Which of the following conclusions is MOST appropriate for the risk practitioner?

options.A: Effective now, but at a low level of maturity
options.B: Ineffective until a written procedure exists
options.C: Mature, with no improvement needed
options.D: Poorly designed and in need of rebuilding

questions.key_concept: Effectiveness shows a control works now; maturity shows it will keep working. A control can be effective yet at low maturity.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the test results show from what the clerk's situation shows.
questions.correct_explanation: The sample shows the reconciliation works today, so it is effective. But it depends on one person with no written procedure, so it would stop if that clerk left or was absent: its maturity is low. The practitioner reports both and proposes documenting and sharing the task. Calling it ineffective is the closest alternative: the gap is about sustainability, not about whether it worked.

wrong_explanations.B: The tests show it worked in every sampled month. Missing documentation threatens whether it keeps working, which is maturity, not current effectiveness.
wrong_explanations.C: Passing tests shows effectiveness, not maturity. Reliance on one undocumented person is a sign of low maturity.
wrong_explanations.D: The design achieved its aim each month. The weakness is how it is sustained, which documentation and cross-training fix without rebuilding it.

tips: Eliminate: C confuses passing tests with maturity, and D calls for a redesign when the design works.
Final two: A beats B because the evidence shows the control works now; dependence on one person threatens how long it will keep working.
Exam cue: effectiveness asks whether a control works now; maturity asks whether it will keep working. Read results for both.
