questions.subtopic: 3C1 Risk action plans. What the draft plan lacks
questions.question: A risk owner at an insurance broker has agreed a draft action plan that lists each action's owner, budget and due date. Which of the following is MOST important to add to the plan?

options.A: The inherent rating from the first assessment
options.B: The risk level the plan is expected to reach
options.C: A weekly status color for each listed action
options.D: The risk practitioner's approval of the plan

questions.key_concept: A risk action plan states the target risk it should reach, so the owner can judge whether it is enough and later whether it worked.
questions.pre_read: Check the plan for how success will be judged, not only how work is scheduled.
questions.correct_explanation: Owners, budgets and dates show how the work will be done, but not what it must achieve. The target risk, the future residual risk the plan should reach, lets the owner judge whether the plan is enough to meet appetite and later test whether it worked. Weekly status colors are the closest alternative: they track progress, but progress toward an undefined level cannot show success.

wrong_explanations.A: The inherent rating is already in the register. It shows the starting point, not where the plan is meant to take the risk.
wrong_explanations.C: Status colors help track actions, but without a target level the plan cannot show whether finishing it is enough.
wrong_explanations.D: The practitioner helps build the plan; the risk owner commits to it. The practitioner's approval adds no authority the owner lacks.

tips: Eliminate: A repeats a starting point already recorded, and D asks the practitioner to approve a plan the risk owner commits to.
Final two: B beats C because a plan needs the level it must reach before progress can mean anything; status colors track activity, not sufficiency.
Exam cue: a treatment plan names owners, actions, resources, dates and the target risk it should reach.

questions.subtopic: 3C1 Risk action plans. Long plan above appetite
questions.question: A manufacturer's 14-month plan to replace unsupported plant-floor servers leaves the risk above appetite until the work ends. What should the risk practitioner recommend the plan include as MOST important?

options.A: Monthly milestones that reveal schedule slippage early
options.B: The plant manager's acceptance of the risk meanwhile
options.C: Interim controls that reduce exposure during the work
options.D: Quarterly progress reports to the IT steering group

questions.key_concept: When a treatment takes months and risk stays above appetite, the plan includes interim measures that reduce exposure meanwhile.
questions.pre_read: Notice how long the risk stays above appetite before the plan finishes.
questions.correct_explanation: For 14 months the risk stays above appetite, so the plan needs interim measures, such as isolating the old servers and closer monitoring, that lower exposure while the replacement proceeds. Milestones are the closest alternative: they show slippage early and belong in the plan, but they do not reduce the exposure the business carries during those months.

wrong_explanations.A: Milestones belong in the plan and show slippage, but they leave the risk above appetite for the whole 14 months.
wrong_explanations.B: A risk above appetite is not the plant manager's to accept alone; it is treated or elevated to whoever set the appetite.
wrong_explanations.D: Progress reports keep IT steering informed, but like milestones they track the work; the exposure stays above appetite for all 14 months.

tips: Eliminate: B has a manager accept a risk above appetite, and D reports progress without lowering the exposure.
Final two: C beats A because interim controls lower the exposure while the work runs; milestones track the work but leave the risk where it is.
Exam cue: a long remediation above appetite needs interim measures, not only a schedule.

questions.subtopic: 3C2 Data collection, aggregation, analysis and validation. Sudden indicator improvement
questions.question: A retailer's KRI for unencrypted laptops fell from 140 to 12 in a month, just after IT moved its data feed to a new device management tool. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Report the improvement to the laptop data-loss risk's owner
options.B: Confirm the new tool covers the same set of laptops
options.C: Lower the laptop data-loss rating in the register
options.D: Reset the KRI thresholds to the new baseline

questions.key_concept: Risk data is validated for completeness and consistency before reporting; a sudden metric change after a source change is checked first.
questions.pre_read: Notice what else changed at the same time as the indicator.
questions.correct_explanation: A drop this large right after a data source change is a reason to check the data before using it. If the new tool sees only enrolled laptops, unencrypted ones may simply be missing from the count. The practitioner confirms coverage and definitions match first. Reporting the improvement is the closest alternative: it is the expected next step, but only once the figure is shown to be real.

wrong_explanations.A: Reporting first passes on a figure that may reflect the tool's coverage, leading the owner to relax about a risk that has not changed.
wrong_explanations.C: Re-rating on an unvalidated metric could lower the rating of a risk whose exposure is unchanged.
wrong_explanations.D: Resetting thresholds builds a possible data error into the indicator, so real exposure could stay hidden.

tips: Eliminate: C re-rates the risk on an unchecked figure, and D builds a possible data error into the thresholds.
Final two: B beats A because data is validated before it is reported; a sudden drop after a source change may mean missing laptops, not fixed ones.
Exam cue: a sudden change in a metric, especially after a data source change, is checked against the source before it is reported.

questions.subtopic: 3C2 Data collection, aggregation, analysis and validation. Data missing at reporting time
questions.question: Two of a bus operator's nine depots have not sent this quarter's KRI data, and the risk report goes to the executive committee tomorrow. What is the risk practitioner's BEST approach?

options.A: Fill the two depots' gaps with last quarter's figures
options.B: Delay the report until the two depots send their data
options.C: Leave the two depots out of the report's totals
options.D: Send the report, stating which depots are missing

questions.key_concept: Risk reports state known data limitations, such as missing units, rather than omitting them, estimating silently or delaying all reporting.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the committee needs to read the totals correctly.
questions.correct_explanation: Decision makers need the report on time and need to know its limits. Sending it with the missing depots named lets the committee read the totals correctly and ask for follow-up. Delaying is the closest alternative: complete data is better, but holding the whole report back denies the committee current information on the other seven depots for the sake of two.

wrong_explanations.A: Last quarter's figures may no longer reflect the two depots. Presenting them as current misleads the committee about present exposure.
wrong_explanations.B: Waiting for complete data delays decisions on the seven depots that did report, when the gap could simply be stated.
wrong_explanations.C: Dropping the depots silently understates the operator's exposure and leaves the committee unaware the totals are incomplete.

tips: Eliminate: A presents stale figures as current, and C silently understates the totals.
Final two: D beats B because a report with its limits stated still supports timely decisions; holding it back costs the committee seven depots' data.
Exam cue: when part of the data is missing, report on time with the limitation stated rather than hiding or guessing.

questions.subtopic: 3C3 Risk and control metrics. Indicator for an access review control
questions.question: Which of the following should a risk practitioner propose as the BEST key control indicator for a bank's quarterly recertification of user access?

options.A: Number of privileged accounts across the bank
options.B: Share of manager recertifications completed late
options.C: Access requests the help desk closed within target
options.D: Insider fraud cases reported in the past year

questions.key_concept: A key control indicator signals that a specific control is weakening, such as reviews completed late.
questions.pre_read: Decide what each measure tracks: exposure, a control, a process or losses.
questions.correct_explanation: A key control indicator shows when a control is weakening. Late recertifications mean access is not being reviewed on time, a direct sign of this control's health that its owner can act on. Help desk closure time is the closest alternative: it is a performance measure of a related process, showing speed of service, not whether access reviews are being done.

wrong_explanations.A: The number of privileged accounts describes exposure, which suits a KRI. It does not show whether the recertification is working.
wrong_explanations.C: Closure within target is a KPI for service speed. Fast provisioning says nothing about whether access is reviewed.
wrong_explanations.D: Fraud cases are a lagging measure of losses. They appear long after a control failure and cannot show which control failed.

tips: Eliminate: A measures exposure, which is a KRI's job, and D counts losses after the fact.
Final two: B beats C because a KCI tracks this control's health; help desk closure time is a KPI for a different process goal.
Exam cue: KRI for exposure, KCI for a control's health, KPI for process performance; match the metric to the question.

questions.subtopic: 3C3 Risk and control metrics. Reset speed offered as risk evidence
questions.question: A university's IT director tells the risk committee that account-takeover risk is low because 98% of password resets are completed within ten minutes. What is the risk practitioner's BEST response?

options.A: Propose a KRI tracking a driver of account takeover
options.B: Ask the service desk to raise its reset target to 99%
options.C: Ask internal audit to verify the 98% reset figure
options.D: Record the reset measure as the takeover risk's KRI

questions.key_concept: A KPI measures process performance; risk exposure needs a KRI tied to a driver of the risk scenario.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the 98% figure actually measures.
questions.correct_explanation: Reset speed is a KPI: it measures service performance and says little about takeover exposure, which depends on drivers such as accounts without multifactor sign-in or exposed credentials. The practitioner proposes a KRI tied to such a driver, with thresholds from tolerance. Verifying the figure is the closest alternative: validation matters, but an accurate measure of the wrong thing still misleads the committee.

wrong_explanations.B: A higher target improves service speed but does not reduce or measure the chance that accounts are taken over.
wrong_explanations.C: Validating data is good practice, but here the problem is the type of measure, not its accuracy.
wrong_explanations.D: Recording a performance measure as a KRI builds the same mistake into the register and future reports.

tips: Eliminate: B improves a performance target that does not measure the risk, and D builds the mix-up into the register.
Final two: A beats C because the measure is the wrong type; checking its accuracy cannot make a KPI warn about takeover risk.
Exam cue: a good KPI does not show a risk is controlled; ask what a measure tracks before accepting it as evidence.

questions.subtopic: 3C3 Risk and control metrics. Human review of AI drafts
questions.question: A hospital requires a doctor to review each discharge summary its AI tool drafts before it goes to the patient. Which of the following BEST indicates that this review control is weakening?

options.A: Summaries the AI tool drafts each working day
options.B: The model's accuracy at its last validation
options.C: Share of drafts approved in under ten seconds
options.D: Patient complaints about discharge summaries

questions.key_concept: A KCI for human review of AI output should show reviewers rubber-stamping, such as very fast approvals, before harm reaches the people affected.
questions.pre_read: Ask how you would know a reviewer had stopped really reviewing.
questions.correct_explanation: A human review reduces risk only if reviewers actually read the drafts. A rising share approved in seconds is an early sign of rubber-stamping, a known risk when people come to trust automated output, so it works as a KCI for the review. Complaints are the closest alternative: they matter, but they arrive after wrong summaries have reached patients, so they warn late.

wrong_explanations.A: Volume shows workload, which may explain rushed reviews, but it does not show whether reviews are being done properly.
wrong_explanations.B: A past validation result describes the model at that time, not the human control now, and it cannot change between validations.
wrong_explanations.D: Complaints are lagging: they appear after wrong summaries reach patients, and many affected patients never complain.

tips: Eliminate: A measures workload rather than review quality, and B describes the model at a past point, not the human control.
Final two: C beats D because fast approvals warn before harm spreads; complaints arrive after wrong summaries have reached patients.
Exam cue: for human review of AI output, watch for signs of rubber-stamping, such as approval time or override rates.

questions.subtopic: 3C4 Risk and control monitoring techniques. Worsening indicator below red
questions.question: Over four months, an insurer's KCI for production changes deployed without an approved ticket rose from 2% to 9%, still below its 10% red threshold. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Wait until the KCI crosses its red threshold
options.B: Ask the control owner to raise the threshold to 15%
options.C: Review the rising trend with the control owner
options.D: Have the risk team approve production changes itself

questions.key_concept: A worsening KCI trend is raised with the control owner before a threshold breach; the risk function challenges but does not run the control.
questions.pre_read: Look at the direction of the indicator, not only its distance from red.
questions.correct_explanation: A steady rise toward the threshold is a warning in its own right. The practitioner takes the trend to the control owner, who is accountable for change approval, to find the cause and fix it before the limit is breached. Waiting for the red threshold is the closest alternative: thresholds trigger escalation, but trend analysis exists so action can start before a breach.

wrong_explanations.A: Thresholds trigger escalation, but by the time this KCI turns red, more unapproved changes will have reached production.
wrong_explanations.B: Raising the threshold to fit current performance hides the decline and breaks the link between the threshold and tolerance.
wrong_explanations.D: The risk team oversees and challenges controls; approving changes itself would make it judge its own work and leave the owner's process unfixed.

tips: Eliminate: B moves the limit to fit the decline, and D has the second line run a first-line control.
Final two: C beats A because a worsening trend justifies action before the threshold; the control owner fixes the cause while there is still margin.
Exam cue: read indicators as trends; a steady move toward a threshold goes to the owner before it is breached.

questions.subtopic: 3C4 Risk and control monitoring techniques. One monitoring cycle for everything
questions.question: A retailer's risk team checks firewall rule changes, critical vulnerability scans and staff background-check records on the same quarterly cycle. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Keep one quarterly cycle for the three checks
options.B: Align each check with the internal audit cycle
options.C: Move the three checks to daily automated runs
options.D: Set each frequency by risk and rate of change

questions.key_concept: Monitoring frequency is set per item by its risk and rate of change, not one cycle for everything.
questions.pre_read: Ask how fast each of the three items changes.
questions.correct_explanation: Monitoring frequency should match how fast each item changes and how much risk it carries: firewall rules and critical vulnerabilities change daily, while background-check records change rarely. Setting each frequency on that basis spends effort where exposure moves. Daily automated runs are the closest alternative: automation helps for fast-changing items, but daily checks of static records add cost without reducing risk.

wrong_explanations.A: A single cycle is simple, but it watches fast-changing firewall rules too rarely and static background checks more than needed.
wrong_explanations.B: The audit cycle is an independent assurance schedule. Monitoring that waits for it leaves fast-changing risks unwatched for months.
wrong_explanations.C: Daily automation suits volatile items like firewall rules, but running it on background-check records adds cost without reducing risk.

tips: Eliminate: A applies one rhythm to items that change at very different speeds, and B ties monitoring to the audit calendar.
Final two: D beats C because frequency follows risk and volatility; daily checks of static records add cost but no protection.
Exam cue: continuous monitoring does not mean constant; set each frequency by risk and how fast the item changes.

questions.subtopic: 3C5 Risk and control reporting techniques. Same cell for three quarters
questions.question: A city council's heat map has shown a supplier-outage risk in the same amber cell for three quarters while its KRI worsened monthly. Which improvement should the risk practitioner recommend as MOST important?

options.A: Trend arrows fed by each risk's indicators
options.B: More cells to give the heat map finer detail
options.C: An average score for the risks in each cell
options.D: A view limited to the risks in red cells

questions.key_concept: Heat maps show position, not trend; reports add KRI-based trend arrows so a worsening risk is not read as stable.
questions.pre_read: Compare what the heat map shows with what the KRI shows.
questions.correct_explanation: A heat map shows where a risk sits, not where it is heading, so a risk can look stable while its drivers worsen. Trend arrows fed by the KRIs let the council's leaders see direction and act before the risk changes cell. Finer cells are the closest alternative: they show position more precisely, but they still hide direction, which is what was missed here.

wrong_explanations.B: Finer cells sharpen position but still give a snapshot; the worsening trend would stay invisible.
wrong_explanations.C: Heat-map scores are ordinal, so averaging them is not meaningful, and it would blur this risk further.
wrong_explanations.D: Showing only red risks would remove this amber risk from view just as it is worsening.

tips: Eliminate: C does arithmetic on ordinal scores, and D removes the worsening risk from view.
Final two: A beats B because the reader needs direction, not finer position; KRI-fed trend arrows show the movement the cell hides.
Exam cue: a heat map is a snapshot; pair it with trend so a stable position is not read as a stable risk.

questions.subtopic: 3C5 Risk and control reporting techniques. Audience for a patching report
questions.question: A risk analyst's monthly report on unpatched checkout terminals at a supermarket chain goes to IT operations, but funding the fix needs the retail director's approval. What is the analyst's BEST change to the reporting?

options.A: Send the full scan results to the retail director
options.B: Copy internal audit on each monthly patching report
options.C: Move the IT operations report to a weekly cycle
options.D: Send it to the retail director with the decision needed

questions.key_concept: Risk reports go to someone with authority to decide on what they show, stating the decision requested.
questions.pre_read: Ask who can approve what the report is asking for.
questions.correct_explanation: A report helps only if it reaches someone who can act on it. Funding the fix is the retail director's decision, so the report should go to the director, in business terms, stating the decision requested. Sending the full scan results to the director is the closest alternative: it reaches the right person, but raw technical detail without the business impact and the decision requested leaves the director unable to act.

wrong_explanations.A: Raw scan results reach the right person in IT's terms, with no decision stated, so the director cannot see what is being asked or why it matters to the stores.
wrong_explanations.B: Internal audit gives independent assurance; copying it does not get the funding decision made by the person who owns it.
wrong_explanations.C: More frequent reports to the same team repeat the problem faster; the team still cannot approve the funding.

tips: Eliminate: B sends the report to assurance rather than to a decision maker, and C repeats it more often to a team that cannot fund the fix.
Final two: D beats A because the director needs the business impact and the decision requested; raw scan results reach the right person in the wrong terms.
Exam cue: report to the level that can decide, in its terms, with the decision requested.

questions.subtopic: 3C6 Monitoring and reporting of emerging risks. Rating a distant threat
questions.question: A risk analyst at an energy retailer reads research suggesting quantum computers could one day break the encryption on billing data kept confidential for 15 years. Which rating approach is MOST appropriate for the register?

options.A: A critical rating until the threat is ruled out
options.B: A range of ratings with stated confidence
options.C: A low rating until a working attack is shown
options.D: The rating a peer firm gave the same threat

questions.key_concept: Emerging risk is rated with ranges and a stated confidence level, then refined as evidence grows, neither ignored nor overstated.
questions.pre_read: Ask how certain anyone can be about this threat today.
questions.correct_explanation: An emerging risk is real enough to record but too uncertain for a single confident score. A range, with the confidence level and assumptions stated and a short review date, tells leaders what is known and lets the rating firm up as evidence grows. A low rating until an attack is shown is the closest alternative: it looks cautious about evidence, but data that must stay confidential for 15 years may be exposed by then.

wrong_explanations.A: Rating it critical without evidence overstates the risk and can pull resources from better-understood risks; emerging risk is reported as uncertain, not certain.
wrong_explanations.C: Waiting for a working attack treats uncertainty as no risk, yet data encrypted now could be copied today and read later.
wrong_explanations.D: A peer's rating reflects its own data and exposure, and borrows its assumptions without stating them.

tips: Eliminate: A treats an uncertain risk as certain, and D borrows a rating built on another firm's exposure.
Final two: B beats C because emerging risk is recorded early with its uncertainty stated; waiting for proof leaves long-lived data exposed meanwhile.
Exam cue: rate emerging risk with ranges and stated confidence, neither ignored nor inflated, and refine it as evidence grows.

questions.subtopic: 3C6 Monitoring and reporting of emerging risks. New AI capability found by scanning
questions.question: Horizon scanning at a parcel carrier finds AI route-planning tools could cut fuel costs 8% but would need customer delivery data shared with vendors. How should the risk practitioner BEST present this to senior management?

options.A: As a threat to block until AI rules are final
options.B: As a tooling choice for the CIO's cost objectives
options.C: As an opportunity with risks weighed against objectives
options.D: As a data-sharing risk for procurement to manage

questions.key_concept: Horizon scanning reports opportunities as well as threats, so leaders weigh a new technology's benefit against its risks.
questions.pre_read: Notice both what the tool offers and what it requires.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk management covers upside as well as downside: the tool supports a business objective, lower cost, while creating data-sharing and vendor risks. Presenting it as an opportunity with its risks lets senior management weigh benefit against exposure and assign an owner. A data-sharing risk for procurement is the closest alternative: the risk is real, but a threat-only framing hides the benefit the decision is about.

wrong_explanations.A: Blocking until rules are final gives up a real benefit on the strength of uncertainty, without weighing the risks against it.
wrong_explanations.B: The CIO can advise on tooling, but the decision affects business objectives and customer data, so it belongs to senior management.
wrong_explanations.D: The data-sharing risk is real, but presenting only the threat leaves out the benefit that management needs to weigh.

tips: Eliminate: A blocks a benefit without weighing it, and B narrows a business decision to an IT tooling choice.
Final two: C beats D because senior management needs the benefit and the risks together; a threat-only view leaves out what is being weighed.
Exam cue: horizon scanning finds opportunities too; present new technology as benefit and risk against objectives, with an owner.
